item.title: How software engineering is changing: a tale of two eras
item.description: We invited readers to write about how building software changed, in an essay challenge. Many of you took part, and today we’re sharing the winning piece from a strong set of entries
item.dc:creator: Gergely Orosz
item.content:encoded:
Before we start: I’m in San Francisco this week and there are a few remaining spots for these live events (registration required):

  • Wednesday (4 Nov): The Pragmatic Engineer Unplugged at the iconic SFJAZZ Center. With Diogo Almeida (creator of Jev & co-inventor of ChatGPT), and Bryan Cantrill (cofounder and CTO of Oxide).

  • Thursday (5 Nov): System Update at The Howard SF. With Karri Saarinen (Linear), Kath Korevec (OpenAI), David Cramer (Sentry) and Adam Rogal (DoorDash)

Also, this week there will be no issue of The Pulse on Thursday. Regular scheduling returns next week!

In September, when The Pragmatic Engineer turned five, I announced an essay challenge, inviting readers to write about how things have changed in tech workplaces and in our projects, for the chance to win a grand prize of $10,000 awarded to our favorite article.

We received 125 submissions, covering a wide range of viewpoints and experiences. Many thanks to everyone who took part. In today’s issue, we publish the winning piece in full.

Congratulations to software engineer Neil Kakkar! We appreciate the sheer volume of data that Neil has collected about how his own output has changed over time. Neil is a dev based in London, with nine years of professional experience; he has interned at Google, and been a software engineer at Bloomberg, Posthog, and Tano. His previous workplace, PostHog, is an open source project, which must’ve been useful for gathering historic data.

In a follow-up issue, we’ll highlight runner-up essays, and link to the ones that impressed us for the effort on show and interesting thoughts.

With that, it’s over to Neil. He covers:

  1. Two eras of shipping. Until last year, he was merging between eight and 20 pull requests (PRs) per month. But since joining an AI-native startup, Neil now ships 200+ PRs per month, approximately a tenfold increase.

  2. Old constraints that disappeared. No more communications overhead or code reviews. The tradeoff: moving faster and breaking things.

  3. New constraints that appeared. Too much context switching (thrashing), losing shared context, pacing yourself is harder, less focus on design, and worries about AI plan limits.

  4. How AI is changing software engineering. Everyone needs to be onboard with AI to get the benefits at work, encouraging experimentation makes a difference, and many existing technologies and processes crack under the change.

I’ve been working at an AI native startup for the past eight months. Before joining Tano, I was at PostHog for four years, a fast moving pre-AI startup, and started my career at Bloomberg, a big fintech private company, where I spent three years. All three workplaces are different: Bloomberg is huge, with 20,000 people and very defined processes. PostHog is smaller, at around 10 people when I joined, and now at 200. At Tano, I was the first engineer and we’re now around 10 people in total.

In each job, I’ve seen what a difference speed and culture make, and more recently, how culture needs to change to keep up with AI.

To back things up, I use in-depth stats about my work at PostHog and Tano. I also have some very rough numbers from Bloomberg. By far, I’ve written more code and made a lot more PRs at Tano than I did at PostHog, and a major part of this is down to AI. Facilitating the shift is engineering culture.

One disclaimer before we get into it: the PostHog stats are from pre-AI. I’ve been following their journey, and PostHog is as “AI-pilled” as it gets now, and output is increasing significantly. In this article, I treat it as a ‘pre-AI baseline’ for excellent engineering work. Tano is a fast-moving AI-native startup, founded after AI agents emerged.

1. Two eras of shipping

Let’s start with some raw numbers. I’m shipping 11x more PRs at Tano than at PostHog, where I shipped 2.4x as many as I did at Bloomberg.

At Bloomberg, I was just starting my career, so I wasn’t the fastest, and moving to PostHog opened my eyes to what a fast-moving startup culture really looks like: we were encouraged to take responsibility, ship things quickly, listen to customers, and solve their issues ASAP.

At Bloomberg and PostHog there was a high bar for code: everything had to be peer reviewed, and as I became senior, I spent a big chunk of my time reviewing code.

PRs can be an easily gamed metric, but I was not trying to game the numbers, so they’re an honest representation of the work done. Below are details of everything I worked on to justify the 11x PR multiplier.

What I worked on

I joined PostHog as a full stack software engineer and worked across the product, from the ingestion pipeline to optimising our analytics queries for funnels and retention on Clickhouse, scaling it up to handle a billion+ events scale, and eventually building out the experimentation product from scratch. I later led the Feature Success team, where we built out two new products: surveys and early access features, while improving experimentation and feature flags.

I joined Tano as a founding engineer and focused on a similar breadth of product as at PostHog, but all compressed into eight months instead of 45. I built out our new affiliate platform, made our content monitoring system a lot more efficient, and did some big migrations, like moving the entire agent architecture to a new system with persistent memory, better tools, and superior observability.

Here’s a summary of work I did at both companies:

How I work today

At PostHog until late 2024, the extent of AI was tab completion. It was great for automating menial work like repetitive test cases, but was a long way away from today’s autonomous agents that can build an entire feature with no human input.

When I joined Tano this year, Claude Code Desktop was already present with really good agent support, and could build out entire features with little hand-holding. I never got used to the command line interface (CLI), and stuck to Claude Code Desktop. I really like the integrated browser and let Claude control it, rather than with my own browser where it’s very annoying if Claude takes over and blocks me from working. Over the last year, the desktop version has caught up to the CLI in features, and has some, like the browser, that a CLI doesn’t directly have.

At any one time, I’m working on 3-5 different things. I start by running through the plan, but mostly let the agent run until it has a PR ready and the comments addressed. Then I run through what it did via a digestible HTML artifact which Claude has instructions to generate with every PR. It looks something like this:

My agents can take 1-2 hours to run. This is for building a full feature, end to end, and given all of the machinery of reviews, verification, and screenshots, it usually takes my agents that long. The run can go even longer if I’m doing a research task that requires investigating a lot of data, processing of images and videos, or iterating towards a goal. I don’t yet use cloud agents because the native Claude agents seem too limited to run things as you would locally.

Larger companies have invested in building their own cloud agents where these integrations are present. It makes sense for them, but not so much at our scale – just yet.

2. Old constraints that disappeared

Eleven times more PRs per month at Tano wouldn’t be possible without AI; I couldn’t write 100k+ lines of code a month by hand, let alone think through that many things. Furthermore, distractions during a normal work day – like new bugs, small feature requests, emergency incidents – break flow and decrease productivity. With AI, these can be passed onto a parallel work thread and not take up focus, front and centre.

How much does the 11x multiplier stack because of everything else, apart from AI? Imagine visiting a pre-AI PostHog where reviews are mandatory as a time traveller from 2026, and you’re the only engineer there with secret access to AI tech from the future. At best, I think you’ll hit a 1-2x productivity gain because the bottleneck shifts from writing to PR approvals – but only for you. Others still aren’t free to review your completed PRs, and your PR output being much faster makes the review queue longer.

At Tano where we’re shipping 10x more, bottlenecks like this and others appear, like communicating with colleagues about what you’re doing, reviewing code, and figuring out what to build next. Let’s talk about some of these.

Communication overhead: How engineering works together

Engineers at Tano work as independently as possible. We come together and talk through big architecture decisions that affect the whole product, but for most things, there’s enough trust at the company that I can go do what I think is best. They also trust that if I’m not sure about what to do, or if there’s risks involved, that I’ll flag the risks and account for trade-offs.

A big part of moving fast is having just one person responsible for things. Of course, this assumes that they can figure out how to do it themselves, and go ship it.

At PostHog, when building out surveys, two engineers and one designer worked together to ship V1 in a month. All three of us iterated on the design, backend, and frontend. When I discovered something that needed to change on the backend, it often meant the other engineer needed to change something on the frontend as well. This was the communication overhead. Even so, engineers who worked together went faster than I would, figuring out the backend, then building out the frontend, and then iterating over any new constraints.

Now that writing code is faster, a communication overhead makes little sense. If I imagine that we’d be building the same survey functionality today, it’s now a lot more efficient if one person owns the entire stack end-to-end; design, frontend, backend. With Claude Code, this is doable by one engineer.

There’s still value in talking about unknown unknowns and things I’m not sure about with other engineers, but where the output is mostly known and it’s a straightforward feature or product, then I think one person working solo is more effective.

Code reviews

Code reviews are optional at Tano. That is, they are optional once you have a handle on the codebase. The time to confidence is variable, depending on how quickly you can get onboarded and how quickly human PR review comments go down to zero. I felt comfortable enough three weeks after I started, but depending on experience it varies, going up to eight weeks.

I built a code review agent via Claude Code Github Actions that runs on every PR, which is now standard across the codebase for everyone and runs in continuous integration (CI). There’s also a deeper, stronger agent we can run on demand if there’s a risky change.

In most cases, this automated reviewer is the only review on PRs. There are no human PR reviews.

Sometimes, things break. For example, in one reporting update, we needed to deal with minor currency units, like cents in the dollar. The agent decided to take these minor units, parse them as floats, and multiply by 100.

Do you see the mistake?

If you’ve worked with financial systems, you’ve probably been here. It’s a dumb mistake to assume every currency has 100 minor units. For example, the minor unit of the Bahraini dinar is the fulūs, and one dinar is 1,000 fulūs. But the generated code assumed it was 100 and this caused issues!

Plus, we already had a utility to handle all currency calculations and a human reviewer would have caught the generated code not using it.

We’re willing to make the trade-off between automated agent review & moving quickly and fixing things as they break. We make it at the cost of not going through a solid human review for every PR because we can do forward fixes on these issues quickly. In this case, we noticed the issue soon after deployment that reporting numbers were not matching up, and fixed them within the hour.

Sometimes, things break in new ways. For example, our posts table in Postgres was getting large, at about 25 GB and 6 million rows. We wanted to add a new partial index to this table, and migrations at 5 million+ rows aren’t straightforward. We realised this a bit later, when we did a blocking migration that blocked writes, and our ingestion pipeline stopped saving new posts. It also timed out, so new deploys failed to run. Now, every such migration needs to happen concurrently, which ensures it doesn’t block deploys or writes to the table.

We make sure to add any new way that things can break to the review agent. Now, it has a list of the largest tables and doesn’t allow blocking migrations on them.

Given no code reviews and only agents writing the code, how has it changed velocity, PR-revert rate, and the median size of PRs? I have some interesting data. The revert rate is 6x lower at Tano because we fix things forward most of the time, rather than revert. But another part of it is that automated code reviews and agents are writing more bug-free code as the models improve.

Since I don’t have to wait for anyone to merge my PRs, the median time to merge is less than an hour.

“Context-maxxing” what to build

At Bloomberg, I was shielded from customers and interacted only with our product manager who helped us prioritise what to work on. Having a clear-cut distinction between engineers and product managers is great when working at huge companies, but these roles merge as workplaces get smaller. At Bloomberg, every team of engineers had a dedicated product manager. At PostHog, there was one product manager for several teams. At Tano, there are none.

The product managers at PostHog helped with lots of research and setting of the product direction, but engineers were also expected to dive in, talk to customers, do our own research, and form our own opinions on product direction as and when needed. I thrived in that environment.

In my current role, I am the product manager, too. We have a roadmapping session every Monday where everyone comes up with issues they’ve faced, things we need to fix, things that will become a problem soon, such as the number of support tickets per customer increasing – which means that as we get more customers, humans could not keep up with the number of tickets to solve.

The CEO and CTO provide the most context on things to be done, and usually have a better idea of prioritisation. They give engineers context on things like customer churn risk, features needed for a new sale to close, etc. Together, we decide what makes sense to tackle, then divide the work among engineers. Usually, every engineer picks up a separate thing to work on.

What used to take a month now often takes a week. This is because agents build things much faster, and I’m typically working on multiple projects at the same time, and no longer have to wait on a product manager to feed me items to build. Hence, we just share context and priorities, and go build things to achieve our weekly goals.

Move fast and break things

Over my career, I’ve been part of five big migrations; one at Bloomberg, one at PostHog, and I’ve led three at Tano.

At PostHog, the big migration took a year. It was about person-on-events. We have two huge tables at PostHog: the events table, with 20 billion+ events of what some anonymous id did; the persons table, which stores persons and their properties. When building funnels or unique user queries, we needed to join these two tables, then aggregate by the person. These queries were very slow, and downright unusable for larger customers. The person-on-events migration moved the person identifier and properties onto events, alongside the anonymous id. It was a massive company-wide effort to update every query to not use joins.

This person-on-events migration was very painful, and all of the code updates were written by hand. We took the time to make sure we future-proofed it because doing another similar migration on events was unfeasible.

At Tano, we finished two complex migrations in just a few weeks. Tano is an influencer marketing agency that builds AI agents to talk to creators, negotiate with them, go through content review with them, then pass it on to brands for final approval so that content can go live. The first iteration of this agent was a free-form checklist of what we wanted the agent to do, and lots of tools for it to accomplish those things. We didn’t have good observability in this system, and the agent would get pretty confused from time to time, using the wrong tool. The solution was to move to a workflow where each task is well defined with its own limited set of tools.

The migration at Tano moved every creator over to the new workflow, mapping existing checklist items into workflow tasks, and building new agent tools for each workflow. As we scaled this system over time, we realised the agent often lacked context on multiple threads with the same creator. The next migration addressed these deficiencies. Both these migrations took weeks, instead of a year.

How fast we want to move is a conscious decision now. In the second migration, I missed some guardrails, which led to creators getting paid twice for the same work. Duplicate payments are not great, but moving fast and breaking things was a trade-off we were very willing to make because getting the new architecture in place meant we could scale faster. At PostHog, we didn’t have the option to migrate quickly.

Our product architecture went from a mostly irreversible decision to a reversible one, which changes the calculus of what kind of experiments you can run, what kind of products you can build, and how specialised they can be for specific clients. We don’t need to get every detail right at the beginning, and can optimize for more information in production, then quickly iterate based on that information.

3. New constraints that appeared

Of course, not everything is ideal with an AI-native work culture. I’ve gone into what’s possible with it, and now I’m going to focus on its costs. The bottlenecks aren’t gone, they just move on to me. Fast-paced work comes at the real cost of exhausting myself quickly, keeping a lot more things in my head, how easily new things distract me, and how little I know about what everyone else is working on.

Building in parallel

I’m almost always working on multiple projects at once. Working on more than one at a time involves a fair amount of context switching, and I find it can get hard to keep up with all the PRs generated by my agents. I limit the number of things I work on at the same time, but it still feels a lot more mentally draining and exhausting than it was before AI agents.

In the charts above, notice how the columns representing multiple things touched in a month are much fuller at Tano than at PostHog. I feel more mentally tired at the end of each day than I used to.

Thrashing

Since things are so easy to fix and build now, I notice engineering is becoming a lot more reactive. A new issue comes in, and immediately I fire a Claude session up to fix it because I know that it won’t take more than an hour end to end, with no real active input from me.

I used to be much more careful about choosing to work on something new. For example, at PostHog, I’d make a measured decision based on the criticality of an issue, and how it competed on priority with my sprint goals. And at Bloomberg, I wouldn’t hear about new work to do at all until a sprint planning session.

In computer science, thrashing occurs when a system spends most of its time switching between tasks, rather than doing them. The fix is to limit concurrency and get the highest priority tasks done first.

Thanks to working on a lot more things, I get pulled in so many different directions that I’m reacting to everything and fixing new bugs that come up day-to-day, instead of what I should be doing. Like a computer, I’m spending more time switching between tasks and getting bugs fixed, than focusing on my own sprint goals.

Sometimes, when bugs are critical, changing priorities is valid and useful. But when I do it just because each individual task doesn’t take long, then it’s not great at moving the company forward.

It’s no wonder that the thrashing problem makes context-maxxing worse. I end up more mentally exhausted because I picked up more work in fixing quick bugs, when I should’ve been working on sprint goals.

Losing shared context

Since there are no more code reviews, I’ve stopped reviewing most code as well. Of course, we review our own code and new team members’, but seldom for experienced colleagues.

Code reviews used to be one of my favourite things at PostHog. I had a feed of every PR coming in and I read them all. Reading helped me keep context of what everyone was working on, and I could jump in to help where needed, i.e., by suggesting things that already might exist in another part of the codebase. As PostHog grew from 20 to ~100 people, the number of new PRs per working day also grew from 15 to 30. It was impossible to keep reading every PR.

At Tano, we are merging about 30 PRs a day as well, and I’m not a big outlier. Another engineer at Tano has very similar output, and newer engineers + CTO are at roughly a third of that because of being new or having other responsibilities.

Having no time to read all PRs means missing context across the business. Doing code reviews was one way I used to keep up with what other engineers were doing, and how the product was growing. Also, isolated contexts affect team culture, as we end up working in silos and this discourages collaboration. On the upside, one person owns big patches of the product and can move fast. On the downside, it also means only one person has that context.

In software engineering, the “bus factor” is the number of people who need to disappear from a project in order for it to stall. If only one person has the context for the project, the bus factor is one. Having a low bus factor is an open problem for every team I’ve worked on. With AI, I do alone what my whole team used to do, which makes the bus factor problem more acute. I think AI provides the solution: if I’m good at writing down context in AGENTS.md files in my product areas, anyone can hit the ground running, learn with AI, and contribute.

The difference is even more striking when I visualize it as the ratio of PRs reviewed, divided by PRs merged:

Pacing myself

Writing code used to define how my day looked at Bloomberg and PostHog. I’d spend time writing code in the morning, open PRs in the afternoon, and get them merged once I got approvals on them. As you can see in the graph below, I opened most of my PRs at PostHog between 10 AM and 3 PM and then waited for approvals, then got them merged later in the day.

At Tano, this graph is a lot more diffuse. PRs go up as and when the agent finishes working, and I then review the code, depending on risk profile and context. I instruct the agent, talk to it about what to build, read a lot more code, and merge much more often throughout the day, and I need to pace myself well.

At Tano, we have core working hours of 9AM to 6PM and many work longer. Early on when I joined Tano, I wanted to get as much done as possible, which led to front-loading tasks in the morning, running several workstreams at once, and multitasking. I’d get mentally exhausted by 3PM and have nothing left in the tank. Before Tano, I was constrained by my speed at writing code, and I can’t write two different lines of code at the same time, so I couldn’t multitask.

I learned to pace myself. This was in order to prioritise the most important tasks, not multitask ten things at once, and to not try and do everything in the morning. If I try doing important changes in the evening when mentally drained, I make mistakes and don’t catch issues I otherwise would.

Working habits

Every evening, I leave my laptop at work and let my agents run locally. They usually stop an hour or two later, so when I come in in the morning, my PRs are ready to go. The difference in morning PRs is clearest in the graph below. At Tano, between 9 and 11 AM, I open 18% of my PRs, while at PostHog, it was only 9%. Except in early mornings and during lunch, the percentage of PRs per hour opened at Tano is pretty stable at roughly 11% per hour because the agents run all day. PostHog peaked around lunch time, and variance throughout the day got slightly larger because as evening approached, my efficiency at writing code went down, so I reserved some time for other tasks, like reviewing code, admin work, and catching up on Slack memes.

PostHog was fully remote, so I’d work from home with no proper end-time for work. My laptop was always with me, and I’d spend some evenings working late because I wanted to get something done, rather than think about it all night. At Tano, I always leave my laptop open at work and I switch off at home. Leaving my laptop at work was a bit weird to colleagues, but it’s been amazing for me: not only do my agents keep running like I want them to, but more importantly, I have a clear switching-off point for the end of the day.

I put this guardrail in place to stop being overwhelmed by AI. Sometimes I do feel that I’m not living up to my potential with AI; it’s here, waiting to be used, waiting to build more things with, waiting for direction, and I’m sleeping? The sense of not doing enough while working harder than ever feels overwhelming.

My guardrails – like no work laptop at home – save me from getting carried away. Routines like always ending the work day at 6pm help me stay grounded. It took a while to come to terms with the feeling of not living up to my potential, but I’ve accepted and reframed this feeling: there’s more to life than just building.

I can be more ambitious with the things I want to build, and I should prioritise what to build over building absolutely everything just because that’s possible now. For example, I recently started a new pseudo-anonymous Instagram AI animations channel, which takes ideas from my blog and converts them into cool animations. I always wanted to make animations, but found it too time-consuming. I’m focusing on this side project over the music generator, reel editor, podcast app, and tv streaming app I also want.

Design

Among the first ten hires at PostHog, one was an artist, and one a designer. Both are heavily responsible for the quirky, well designed, beautiful brand that is PostHog.

With AI, I observe early-stage startups discounting design work. I assume they do so because AI can do a good-enough job at making things look nice. But at the same time, AI designs are very similar to a lot of other designs out there. Neo-brutalist design tries to stand out, but most AI-generated neo-brutalist design is still pretty similar. At Tano, it’s what we’ve ended up with, and we’re taking steps to figure out what our brand should look like.

Hitting AI limits

Tokenmaxxing is the idea of using as many AI tokens as possible, often with no regard for the actual productivity gains of doing it.

At Tano, there is no ‘infinite’ AI budget. Everyone has one 20x Claude Max plan subscription, and that’s it.

We don’t have infinite funding, and use AI as a tool to help us move faster instead of it being an autonomous teammate. If we were paying API rates, my usage would come to $8,000+ per month.

Hitting limits on my Claude max plan does still happen. It is more frequent when experimenting with using AI as an autonomous teammate running loops and fixing any errors it finds from our logs. Hitting the limit forces me to focus on what’s the most important thing to be doing.

Weirdly, I want more out of my tools. I’m already shipping 11x more thanks to AI, but why stop there? I want to explore what’s possible if I had no token limits: how effective is Claude at running autonomously, watching logs, session recordings on PostHog, and acting on this information by opening PRs on its own? Can it monitor agent behaviour at Tano, read every conversation with every creator, and tell us when we paid one creator twice because of a bug in our migration?

Already, AI agents are writing my code. But some seem far more capable if you have the tokens to spend. How much further can I push them? I don’t know the answer yet, but it’s something I would love to experiment further on.

Overall, it seems like the world is changing very quickly, and I’m super excited to be in the middle of it all.

4. How AI is changing software engineering

So, how much of the change is due to AI, and how much is from everything else around it?

AI is a speed multiplier. Speed is a defining feature of start ups, and how they outcompete incumbents by experimenting and adapting to market demand quickly, and catching up to incumbents in terms of features. PostHog was not the first product analytics platform – in fact, it was ten years late to the party. But people at PostHog executed quickly, caught up with the competition, and the product has now expanded into several different categories, like experimentation, data warehouse, error tracking, and session recordings.

We built these products before AI. Today, a startup with AI can out-execute another without AI, and since speed is a defining feature, the startup without AI will have a very difficult time.

Your productivity gains are limited if the rest of the company is not onboard with AI. It’s clear that AI is necessary, but it’s not sufficient. For example, if you were a time-traveller visiting PostHog, pre-AI, you’d still not be all that productive with all of today’s AI tools. This is because with mandatory code reviews from fellow engineers, the review queue keeps increasing endlessly since we produce faster than we can review.

Encouraging experimentation in ways of working can pay off. I’ve seen teams with this approach end up better off. A team like Tano encourages experimentation by not frowning upon me for leaving my laptop at work and letting agents run overnight.

Further, a company that is flexible, recognises new constraints when they show up, and works towards removing them so it can move even faster, seems to do better than ones that adopt one way of working and stick to it. For example, Anthropic also automated code reviews away, but then ended up constrained by continuous integration (CI) pipelines. They unblocked CI as the new constraint and then found out their source control couldn’t keep up. In order to keep moving faster, they redesigned source control.

As you adopt AI to move faster, a lot of working technologies and team processes will crack. At the very least, they will strain under the load of getting more work done. A lot of startups will probably not end up at the scale where they have to redesign source control, but the general principle stands: you can restrict AI for what I believe suboptimal results, or you can lean into it, find out where new constraints end up – like in code reviews – and relax those constraints by automating those reviews so you can continue moving faster.

I value a team culture where we experiment, are open to being proven wrong, humble, curious, and try to make the most of the tools we have. At Tano, this culture is a defining factor in our successful AI adoption, and I believe culture is a necessary – and sufficient – condition of success at every AI-era startup.

Takeaways

Gergely, again.

Thanks to Neil for this data-driven essay on how he sees things changing in the industry, and how quickly it’s happening.

Neil’s story about how his PR output increased tenfold from the beginning of the year is an interesting one. Two forces are at play:

  • Since January, the industry has started to adopt AI coding agents more. We’re seeing around a twofold increase in PR output on average, across the industry, as covered in our deepdive on PR frequency and AI cost

  • Neil moved from a startup that was fast-moving in the pre-AI era (PostHog) to an even younger, truly “AI-native” startup where nothing could be put at risk by moving too fast

I appreciate this contrast.

The sudden change in shipping pace when going from a pre-AI startup to an AI-native one is hard to ignore. Of course, we know that iteration speed is pretty meaningless by itself, without looking at things like finding product-market-fit, generating revenue, or having healthy unit economics.

Still, I wonder if this new generation of “AI-native” startups have this temporary advantage of iterating much faster than companies that are only a few years older than they are. I have no doubt that “pre-AI” startups will eventually catch up, but when you have a business that works well, you want to be more careful and deliberate in changing your processes and tooling. The last thing you want to do is to break your business by being careless!

I also like that Neil talks a lot about the pressure that comes with using AI. He feels the need to put several guardrails in place, so that he has personal time to unwind and come back refreshed and focused. This is positive because it’s really easy to use AI too much and never stop working: in March, we talked about this “Dracula-effect” with Steve Yegge, including how using AI agents seems to drain the energy of engineers.

Congratulations to Neil once more for his personal, highly detailed account of what’s changed in his work. Thanks to everyone who took part in this essay challenge! Look out for more essays to come.

item.title: The Pulse: Anthropic kills the coding interview
item.description: AI is rendering the Leetcode-style interview pointless and now Anthropic has deleted it from its interview loop. Also: details of incident.io’s AI spend, Microsoft’s exit offer to engineers, and more
item.dc:creator: Gergely Orosz
item.content:encoded:
The Pulse is a series covering events, insights, and trends within Big Tech and startups.

Today, we cover:

item.title: Software engineering at Google & CS education with Titus Winters

item.content:encoded:
Before we start: I’m in SF this week and next, hosting these free-to-attend events (registration required). If you’re in the area, hopefully I'll see you at one of them:

  • The Pragmatic Engineer Unplugged: Wednesday (4 Nov), 5pm-7:30pm. With Diogo Almeida (creator of Jev & co-inventor of ChatGPT), and Bryan Cantrill (cofounder and CTO of Oxide). We still have space left, RSVP here.

Listen and watch now on YouTube, Apple, and Spotify. See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom.

Brought to You by

• turbopuffer – The tpuf eng team is completely redesigning their storage architecture from first principles. And they’re documenting all of it! They made epic progress, take a look: turbopuffer.com/v3

• Linear – one of the big challenges for us devs is the sheer amount of code to review. Linear Diffs is a new feature to review PRs inside of Linear, with all the context in one place. It also supports stacked PRs. Check it out

• WorkOS – WorkOS built Airlock, the authorization layer for AI agents. It evaluates every request against the agent’s intent + your rules and either allows it, denies it, or routes it to a human. Works with Claude Code, Codex & MCP gateways. Give it a spin

In this episode

An engineer who helped create today’s software engineering curriculum now says to burn down almost all of it. What’s the cause of this contradiction? We find out from the lead author of Software Engineering at Google.

Titus Winters spent more than a decade at Google, where he led its readability program and built Abseil, Google’s open-sourced foundational C++ libraries. He is currently a Senior Principal Scientist at Adobe, where he focuses on developer experience and productivity.

In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Titus and I discuss how his team tackled a massive refactoring project across Google’s 250-million-line C++ codebase, why Google made testing mandatory, and his work on updating the ACM/IEEE undergraduate computer science curriculum guidelines.

We also explore why traditional productivity metrics miss some of AI’s biggest benefits, what needs to change in CS education, and how new engineers can stand out.

Takeaways from the conversation with Titus

Titus is a deep thinker and has worked on some very interesting projects. Here are 12 things that stick out to me from our chat.

1. Was refactoring 250M+ lines of C++ code the largest refactoring task of all time? This happened at Google in 2010, a few months after Titus joined the search giant. An internal email asked for volunteers to help clean up old C++ code, some of it written by the very first Googlers.

A team of a dozen people was assembled. Google had close to 250M lines of code at the time, edited by 10,000 engineers. Titus recalled the cleanup: “We were replacing the foundation of the Empire State Building. We were not allowed to close the building or block traffic. Oh, and we discovered nuclear waste in the basement.”

2. The refactoring was done with advanced language parsing techniques, long before LLMs existed. Back in 2010, there were no LLMs for this giant refactor. Here’s what the team did:

  • Parse: ran a MapReduce over the whole codebase. The mapper parsed every build target into an abstract syntax tree

  • Match: match exact call patterns in the tree

  • Code generation: generated edits to be made by the machine

  • Coexist: make the old API and new API work side-by-side

  • Shard: once the new API is ready to go, split the edits by directory, and send them out in batches

  • Block the old: make sure nobody copied the old pattern back into the code

  • Delete: remove the old API

The clang-format toolkit exists because Titus and his team needed it for this refactor.

3. Google made automated tests mandatory after Search could no longer ship regularly. Around 2007, Search, the flagship product, was unable to ship at a monthly cadence any more, and the best they could ship to production was quarterly.

Almost every change at Google touched Search’s code, even things like a change to Gmail. To clamp down, Google, as an org, mandated that every change was to be accompanied by a test. Over time, Search returned to its former higher cadence.

4. Google’s readability program might have been the largest educational program ever in tech. To make a code change at Google, two people need to sign off that change through a code review:

  • An “owner” of the file/project: someone on the team with domain knowledge

  • A “readability” reviewer: an engineer certified to be a “readability” expert in the given language that the change was made in

Google’s first engineer, Craig Silverstein, walked each new dev hire through their first change. Java teams turned this approach into mentoring, where experienced reviewers were assigned to review all changes in a round-robin fashion. And soon enough, a formalized readability program was built for all languages. When Titus left Google three months ago, 10,000+ engineers were enrolled in readability at any given time. Has there ever been a bigger engineering “classroom” anywhere else?

5. Fear is not an acceptable basis for engineering. Titus believes your codebase is unsustainable if it’s not possible to make a valuable change safely. There shouldn’t be fear about making a change to a codebase. Having the right “security nets” that catch errors is strategically very valuable because it enables teams to make changes without fear.

6. With AI, outages seem to be going up. Titus talks to engineers at other companies and it’s the same picture: code output is up hugely versus a year ago, and outages are also up about 30%, while the number of features shipped is static. It seems like treading water. From that angle, it’s not positive for AI; based on outages alone, the technology could be a negative.

7. On the other hand, AI makes ambitious projects possible that weren’t realistic without it. Titus is optimistic about AI as a net productivity boost, and reckons people are caring about the wrong things. He sees the real value of AI as not in repeating the same things as before at higher speed. Instead, it’s about doing things you never thought of before: projects so ambitious that they didn’t used to make sense!

8. Burn down the US undergrad CS curriculum (most of it). Titus was the only working engineer on the steering committee for the ACM/IEEE/AAAI CS curriculum guidelines in 2023, and believes the curriculum is hopelessly out of date. He accuses it of not having altered substantially since around 2000, while the industry has. Testing and verification are cited as mattering a lot more for new joiners, but they are absent from the curriculum.

Unless major changes are made to make it relevant, computer science enrollment could fall and software engineering programs that focus on practical dev skills will be attractive to students – this is Titus’s forecast.

9. “Middle group” of students struggle most with AI. Professors in CS programs tell Titus that students divide into three groups:

  • The best are better than ever and take full advantage of a patient, knowledgeable tutor, aka the AI

  • The middle: professors say that everyone below the “best” have collapsed: students below a B grade tend to not understand code at all

  • The weakest: they can catch up to the middle of the pack easier – mostly by producing slop with AI, though.

When I did a guest lecture at my alma mater, professors told me similar observations – how the “middle of the pack students,” by grades, have disappointingly low understanding of the subject, compared to former years.

10. Grading students’ prompts and tests is better than focusing on their code. Titus would focus on the thinking processes students put into building and validating software, not just the output.

11. “Remember Andrew’s axe” – advice for junior engineers. Andrew chops down a tree with an axe. Or did Andrew’s axe chop down the tree? Titus says Andrew is the one who did it, and the axe is only a tool for his will. Similarly with AI: it’s a tool for you to use, and anthropomorphizing this tool takes us out of that mindset.

12. To succeed, don’t copy what everyone else is doing! As our time came to an end, I asked Titus what he’d say to sophomore students. It’s a segment that did not make it into the podcast, but I’m adding it here!

“Most of my success in life has come from not doing the thing that everyone else is doing. It is really incredibly hard to stand out if you are just listening to what is a hot topic and chasing the same shiny thing that literally everyone else is doing.

My primary advice [is to] find something that you love that is not just the same thing that you assume is on everybody’s resume, and do a lot of that. Find a passion project, go really deep on it.

Like, ‘how do I use computing and AI vibe coded new generation techniques?’ ‘How do I solve this problem that matters a lot to me?’ ‘Or how do I express myself through a game or art?’ The more that you do [something] that’s uniquely you, the more that you stand out, and the more that you do, the more that you learn.”

item.title: AI SRE: what is it, how could it change on-call – and does it work?
item.description: “AI SRE” is fast becoming a trending term fueled by flashy demos from vendors, but has an AI SRE ever really been on-call while engineers slept? Deepdive
item.dc:creator: Gergely Orosz
item.content:encoded:
Before we start: I’m in San Francisco this week and also next week. On Wed, 4 November, I’m hosting The Pragmatic Engineer Unplugged at the iconic SFJazz Club, featuring a rare conversation with Diogo Almeida (creator of Jev & co-inventor of ChatGPT), and Bryan Cantrill (cofounder and CTO of Oxide). It’s free to attend with registration, sign up here.

In May 2025 at Microsoft’s annual BUILD conference, the tech giant introduced “Azure SRE Agent” with an onstage demo in which an alert fired and the AI SRE Agent went to work on identifying the root cause, and then shipped a fix, all without having to wake up a human dev oncall.

Watching this demo, the whole thing felt artificial to me, and I failed to imagine any engineering team at Microsoft – or anywhere else! – letting an AI make production decisions with no human oversight that could potentially cause a worse outage. And sure enough, after last year’s BUILD I heard no more about “SRE agents” at Microsoft or elsewhere – until recently, that is.

Now, I do hear it being mentioned: OpenAI built an AI SRE bot called Sevbot, and last month, an engineer at ING bank told me they’re working on their own, in-house AI SRE. Just as visibly, at tech conferences I’ve attended, AI SRE vendors’ stands have been popping up in numbers.

To find out what’s going on, we reached out with Jessica to three of the most popular AI SRE startups/AI incident platforms to hear directly from them: Rootly, incident.io, and ResolveAI (note: I’m an investor in incident.io). Thanks for all the input!

Today, we cover:

  1. Why is AI SRE “hot”? Incidents and pages are trending upward, thanks to AI agents speeding up at shipping code to production. It only makes sense to invest in better oncall tooling.

  2. What does “AI SRE” mean? It’s mostly about doing incident investigation much faster, and inside of Slack. Whether “AI SREs” should make code changes is debated.

  3. Building an investigation agent. Fanning out multiple agents is common, as is the practise of engineers steering them in Slack or Teams. A “context layer” with a knowledge graph and memory is used for better investigation outcomes. Several tech companies built their own investigation agents instead of relying on vendors.

  4. Making agents accurate. Helpful approaches include verifying incident hypotheses with adversarial agents and a mix of models, as well as running evals and backtesting. However, measuring “accuracy” of AI SREs is tricky and highly specific to each company, and even engineering team.

  5. Making agents fast & affordable. Everyone wants fast, cheap, and accurate AI SREs, but there are tradeoffs. Model routing, lean prompts, and tracking cache hit rate are ways to engineer a system with the right tradeoffs for your constraints.

  6. How long until autonomous agents? The fully autonomous agents demoed on conference stages are still not a reality, but AI agents triaging pager calls – and silencing unimportant ones – is becoming more common. Interestingly, there’s not been much change in this area from how Meta operated its own systems with AI two years ago.

  7. What’s changing for on-call engineers? A new category of AI-related outages is appearing, and engineers should eventually get hit with fewer pages, but the incidents that do reach engineers will be hard. There’s a deskilling risk, and it could be smart to train oncall with incident response simulations like those from Uptime Labs.

As usual, I have no affiliation with vendors mentioned in this article except for my investment in incident.io – mentioned above. I have not been paid to mention any company.

1. Why is AI SRE “hot”?

A year back, there was little to no buzz about AI SREs, but that’s all been changing.

The main driver seems to be that there’s a lot more code deploys. Almost all tech companies have seen their PR frequency double in a year due to AI agents. Let’s do some basic “reliability math”:

i = c x p:
Incident rate = [Change rate] x [Probability]

C = number of changes per unit time
P = probability a single change introduces failure

This says that if we have few deployments (low change rate) and high confidence that each deploy works (low probability of failure), then that is a pretty stable system. But with AI agents, deploy frequency is up and the incident rate is likewise increasing at most companies.

We know that C (the number of changes in a given timeframe) is up twofold or more on last year at many companies, and will probably climb higher. Data from Rootly shows that pages are also up from a year ago, and outside-business-hours pages have nearly doubled:

Broadly, there’s two approaches to lowering P (incident failure rate probability):

  1. Better pre-deploy verification: more testing & verification loops

  2. Learn from incidents: make the system more resilient

Most AI SRE vendors are well placed to learn from incidents and act upon them. For example, here’s Rootly’s high-level strategy for more resilient systems:

2. What does “AI SRE” mean?

“AI SRE” looks on its way to becoming the agreed term for AI-augmented oncall tooling, even though we’ve not spoken to a single person who likes it – and we agree.

AI SRE vendors themselves don’t like it. When we talked with incident.io, Resolve, and Rootly for this article, the reply was that, unfortunately, they’ve not come up with anything better and so this name has come to stick instead. Alternative names proved less sticky even though they’re less inaccurate, like “autonomous reliability agents”, “automated remediation agents”, and “automated incident investigation agents.”

A reason “AI SRE” is less than ideal is as simple as the fact that a site reliability engineer (SRE) does a lot more than just deal with oncall alerts! They work on making a system more reliable in its entirety and a good chunk of that work happens before and after outages.

Despite all that, this article is going with the flow and using “AI SRE” because there’s not much choice, while covering oncall and incident handling tools that are AI-augmented/AI-powered.

We cover more on the SRE profession and reliability engineering in a deepdive with Dave Connor, who worked at Google when the term ‘SRE’ was coined.

AI SRE tools mostly help with the investigation phase of incidents. Tools like Rootly, incident.io, and ResolveAI are most helpful after an alert has fired and an engineer starts investigating. Pre-AI, this investigation phase involved:

  • Alert details: inspect the alert and try to figure out what it means

  • Dashboards: check custom dashboards to confirm whether there’s an alert, which systems are impacted, and where the root cause investigation should start, if so

  • Runbooks: consult runbooks and follow the steps to remedy the issue, if it’s a common one

  • Logs/observability: look through the logs of observability systems like Datadog, Sentry, Honeycomb, etc

These days, AI tools have gotten pretty good at all these tasks if they have sufficient data access. Of the three vendors we talked with, all do their investigations with AI. When building in-house AI SRE tools, starting at the investigation phase is a no-brainer:

Most AI SRE tools speed up the investigation of an incident. incident.io’s agent orchestrator does something similar to when an oncall engineer opens eight tabs to look through what systems might have issues:

  • Orchestration: the main agent decides to kick off an investigation

  • Subagents: it fans out investigation work to subagents which report on progress

  • Heuristics: the orchestrating agent can make speculative calls, then use heuristics to decide where to go deeper

There’s a lot of value in having an oncall engineer join the incident channel roughly five minutes after an alert fires, and to have a summary of investigations by AI agents. It gives the oncall dev a sense of what might be happening, instead of having to do all the “shovel work.”

AI SREs typically interact with devs in Slack. At startups that use Slack for comms, Slack is also the place to coordinate incidents; even pre-AI, it was common to open a dedicated Slack channel for an incident. Most AI SRE tools have a Slack bot in the incident channel; incident.io’s bot sits in the incident channel the whole time and takes steering instructions from engineers (look at the status of a specific system, ask it to dig up specific logs, etc.)

AI SRE tools require a high level of trust, which is a reason to build in-house. For these agents to be effective, they need access to telemetry, observability, logs, even the version control system because the more data they can access, the more effective they are. As Sam Newman writes in his book, ‘Building Resilient Distributed Systems’:

“For tools like incident.io’s AI SRE to work, they need access to information. This means that they will need broad access to a lot of valuable data if you want them to be effective. If the agent can’t see your telemetry data, then it can’t slice and dice that data for you. If it can’t look at your source code repository, then it can’t spot recent commits that may have caused the issue. This does mean that you need a high degree of trust in the vendor creating and running the agent.”

But how much do you trust a third-party vendor with all your data; potentially even a readonly version of your sanitized production database, which could come in handy for some investigations? The larger the company, the less likely that access to highly sensitive data will be granted. The trust issue is a major driver in why many mid-size-and-above companies build their own AI SRE tools.

Even if a vendor offers zero data retention (ZDR), there’s still a risk that its system could be compromised and leak information. Also, a vendor offering ZDR could be at a disadvantage when improving the system, compared to an in-house AI SRE tool that it’s possible to train on the data.

Our take is that AI SRE vendors are likely to become more capable than home-grown solutions because AI SRE startups obsess about better tooling fulltime; success depends on it. At larger companies, an AI SRE tool is more of a novel side project; engineers initially get excited but then move on to newer projects.

Should AI SREs only mitigate, or also remediate? Once the root cause analysis of an outage is done, and the AI SRE agent has helped to mitigate it, is the work complete? On one hand, the AI SRE tool typically also has access to the codebase, so should be able to come up with code-fix suggestions. On the other hand, pre-AI, you hardly ever saw an SRE team raise pull requests to fix the root causes of outages because they didn’t have the context or expertise for systems someone else built. But with AI, context can be passed on and expertise in writing code is pretty common for AI agents.

We asked the three AI SRE startups how they approach writing code to fix root causes, post-incident. They have different ways:

  • Handing off PRs to coding agents. incident.io is focused on passing incident context to engineers’ existing coding agents. The company built and demoed autonomous PR creation at its annual conference last year, but cofounder Chris Evans told us that customers generally prefer to use their own coding setups. The focus is therefore on giving agents the context they need to help engineers implement a fix.

  • A hybrid approach at ResolveAI. The tool writes simple PRs itself and hands over larger changes to the customer’s coding agents.

  • Intend for agents to autonomously merge PRs at Rootly. Their vision is to get to a point where their agent drafts a PR, and another agent judges whether it’s safe to merge, and when deemed safe, the merge happens automatically. If the merge is deemed risky, the oncall engineer still gets woken up. As yet, all PRs raised happen after a human has approved them.

3. Building an investigation agent

All three vendors we talked to have rebuilt their investigation agent at least once because integrating AI into oncall looks simple, but that’s not the case. For example, ResolveAI built three different architectures in two years:

Scripted workflow. In 2024, models could not yet reliably chain tool calls. The startup built a pipeline of specific prompts like: “classify the alert“ → “gather logs+metrics“ → “extract insights” → “rank hypotheses.” This pipeline handled common incidents well, but did poorly when incidents did not “fit the script”.

Single agent with a knowledge graph. In 2025 when tool calling with AI agents became reliable, a primary agent took the alert → looked at a graph of services/dependencies/runbooks/deployments → decided what to do next. Overall, the accuracy improved but new problems appeared:

  • Context rot: for long, multi-service incidents, the agent ran into context saturation (the “dumb zone” as discussed on the Pragmatic Engineer podcast episode with Dex Horthy). It started to request data it already had and to contradict its own conclusions.

  • Self-confirmation: the agent was tasked to grade hypotheses it came up for likely causes of incidents. The agent almost always confirmed its first suspicion and didn’t examine its conclusion.

  • Lack of ‘memory’: lessons from past investigations didn’t carry over to new ones.

Multi-agent system. In 2026, the team came up with three different agent roles:

  • Investigator: chases one hypothesis after another

  • Verifier: challenges the conclusions of investigators. It’s structurally independent of investigators to avoid self-confirmation

  • Communicator: agent updates stakeholders

The Resolve team told us they find this system to be the most reliable and resilient in incident investigations.

A typical investigation

At a high level, all three AI SRE startups follow similar steps for dealing with investigations:

  1. Trigger: an alert fires or an engineer declares an incident

  2. Orientation: pull in relevant data like telemetry and logs to find out what’s changed recently, like deployment and feature flags

  3. Fan out: kick off parallel investigative agents.

  4. Verify: challenge the conclusions of investigative agents

  5. Report: update Slack and other communication channels

  6. Steer: engineers give input to the agent, usually via Slack. This spawns more “fan out” investigations

  7. Hand off: an engineer or coding agent takes on suggested mitigation actions, like making a code change, restarting a system, etc.

There’s plenty of nuance in how to implement each step: our three vendors often do so in distinct ways! Here are tactics for each step:

  • Trigger: how do you categorize alerts: do you give fixed buckets for the agent (e.g. “needs human attention”, “can wait for business hours”, “noise”), or have the agent come up with a hypothesis for the cause before paging a human?

  • Orient: do you measure the potential impact of the page (which can add latency), follow different rules based on the service impacted, or pull in a larger context graph?

  • Fan out: do you fan out by hypothesis/potential failure type, or with as many agents as makes sense? What about long-running agents; do you wait for them, or limit tool-calling depth, or the cost of an investigation agent run?

  • … and so on for other steps. You’ll want to decide on tradeoffs between latency, accuracy, and cost.

Context layer, knowledge graphs, memory

AI SRE tools need some kind of understanding of what the production system looks like: how systems are connected, the dependencies, and what caused things to go down previously. All three AI SRE tools build some kind of “context layer” to help the agent figure out root causes of an incident faster:

  • Rootly calls its Atlas: a combination of a knowledge graph, memory, and AI connectors

  • incident.io calls its Nexus: a combination of catalog, code, telemetry, and past incidents

  • Resolve calls its HiveMind: a combination of context, investigation skills, memory, and actions

Generalizing a bit, all three of these context layers are made up of a knowledge graph, memory, and tools.

Knowledge graph

This is a graph of:

  • Services

  • Data stores

  • Cloud resources

  • Deployments

  • Runbooks

  • Past incidents

  • … and other relevant resources or sources of information

This is not something that only vendors build; practically any team building AI tools can come up with it. For example, Uber built a neat in-house knowledge graph that’s used by most of their AI systems, which we cover in the podcast episode ‘Uber’s AI infra from the inside.’

Memory

Memory is the system for storing information from past investigations. Agents can use this layer to steer the current investigation and memory provides information like:

  • “When latency spikes on payments, the root cause is more often than not with the connection pool”

  • “This specific alert is typically noise the first hour after a deploy from a specific service”

  • etc.

All three AI SRE startups have their own memory layers, but each implements it slightly differently. For example, Rootly has the concepts of:

  • “Activated” memory notes: a note earns its spot in a more important memory note after playing a useful role in an incident, or someone activates it manually

  • “Quarantined” memory notes: if a note is contradicted, it gets quarantined to not be used in the future. Systems keep changing, and this is one way to not feed stale information to the agent

Is it a good idea to pool customers’ incident data? AI SRE vendors have the advantage that they observe more incidents – and very different ones – via customers. Among our three vendors, Rootly is the only one that allows customers to opt into pooling their data in return for getting a hopefully improved agent.

Rootly’s idea is to build a kind of “Stack Overflow for AI SREs” internally. The idea is that Company A’s retrospective – scrubbed of sensitive details – might help Company B resolve an incident faster. Cofounder JJ Tang:

“Most vendors in our space promise your data stays siloed forever. We think that’s the wrong default for operational data. For example, an outage caused by a bad Redis config isn’t a trade secret.”

Sharing of confidential data is a tricky topic. Rootly says it gives customers granular control over what is shared and excluded, and can access shared records and remove them. The scrubbing code is not currently open-sourced, which the company plans to change.

Our take is that benefiting from a “knowledge base” is promising, but contributing to a broader vendor knowledge base needs to be done carefully. Responsible vendors will make contributions easy and transparent. Just ensure that when contributing data, anything confidential is scrubbed first.

Tools

Agents use tools, connectors, plugins, and AI skills to connect to data sources during an investigation. This is pretty similar to how any AI vendor is integrated into a company with the right connectors. Needless to say, all AI vendors expose MCP interfaces, and offer Claude Code/Codex plugins for easy integration with other internal services.

Agents in the Slack channel

AI SREs typically interact with devs in Slack during an incident. Teams is also supported by all three AI SRE startups, and Rootly also supports GChat, but most startups are on Slack. It’s interesting that Slack is becoming the preferred choice for human-to-agent communication of most tech companies.

There are a few challenges these tools need to solve:

  • Length of updates. How concise or verbose should updates by the AI SRE tool be? incident.io played a lot with getting this right: they learned that being too concise makes devs not trust the agent (too few details), whereas being too lengthy can be annoying

  • When to speak up? Rootly designed its agent to be predominantly quiet and to only post when:

    • a question in the channel goes unanswered

    • a stakeholder joins without context

    • someone declares “mitigated” without proof

    • a risky action is announced with no rollback plan

How in-house teams build AI SREs

Lots of medium-sized and larger tech companies build AI SREs in-house, and the big benefit is that they can expose internal context a lot more freely to their agent than to a vendor. My sense is that the AI SREs built by different companies end up being pretty similar in capabilities and structure to those that vendors build.

The AI SRE is a subset of Monzo’s cloud agent, which calls its cloud coding agent ‘Project Chip’. This is the high-level architecture:

Agent Chip is a general, in-house, engineering agent that can be triggered from Slack, Linear, GitHub, and other internal systems. When an incident occurs, Agent Chip has ‘Agent Chip Incident Mode’ invoked and it pulls together context from across systems, surfaces possible causes, and can draft a fix.

Other places have in-house AI SREs:

  • OpenAI: its tool is ‘Sevbot’. It collects details, determines possible mitigations (but never executes any), answers devs’ questions in a Slack channel, and can apply mitigations when instructed

  • Stripe: built its own incident investigation agent that runs on each outage. A simpler run (that tends to collect necessary signals to investigate the outage) takes three minutes, on average. A more thorough deep investigation is 14 minutes long, on average.

  • Google: SREs use ‘ProdAgent’ (Google’s internal agentic incident management framework) within Gemini CLI. It functions like get_incident_details, causal_analysis, timeseries_correlation, log_analysis and others. ProdAgent doesn’t generate code, it only suggests using tools exposed via MCP, like borg_task_restart (Borg being Google’s infra management platform). ProdAgent has policy enforcement and audit trails. It seems less polished, but is built to minimize the risk of messing up production: more scripts, less LLM determinism!

4. Making agents accurate

An engineering challenge of building AI SRE tools is that they need to be right most of the time, even when built on models prone to confabulation and which change often.

item.content:encoded:

item.title: The revised rules of engineering management with Will Larson
item.description: Will Larson, CTO of Imprint, explores how AI and shifting industry expectations are changing engineering management, career ladders, and the path from engineer to CTO.
item.dc:creator: Gergely Orosz
item.content:encoded:
Before we start: I’m very excited to announce an The Pragmatic Engineer Unplugged live event: with Diogo Almeida (the creator of Jev) and Bryan Cantrill (cofounder and CTO, Oxide). 4 November (Wednesday), San Francisco, the SFJAZZ Center. It’s free to attend, but spaces are limited and registration is required.

Stream the latest episode

Listen and watch now on YouTube, Apple, and Spotify. See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom.

Brought to You by

• turbopuffer – vector and full-text search built on object storage: fast, 10x cheaper, and extremely scalable. Under the hood, the team are rewriting the tpuf storage engine. Follow along until it hits production at turbopuffer.com/v3

• What if you only needed a single test to harden your system? Get a free introduction to property-based testing: through a live, online webinar hosted by Hillel Wayne (a recent podcast guest), author of Logic for Programmers and Developer Educator at Antithesis. RSVP here.

• Entire – Git hosting, rebuilt for the agentic era. Entire hosts your code in-region, and is up to 89x faster than any other competitor. Mirror from GitHub with a single click – I’ve already done so.

In this episode

What’s changed in “the unwritten rules” of engineering management since the 2010s, why are hands-on managers “back”, and what has it done to the engineer-to-CTO career path? Today’s guest is one of the best people I know who can tackle these questions.

Will Larson is CTO of Imprint, was an engineering executive for 10+ years, and is the author of several popular books on engineering leadership, including ‘The Engineering Executive’s Primer,’ ‘Staff Engineer, An Elegant Puzzle,’ and ‘Crafting Engineering Strategy.’ Previously, he was also CTO at Carta and Calm, and an engineering leader at Stripe and Uber.

In this episode, we explore how engineering leadership has evolved from management practices shaped in the long post-financial-crisis ZIRP era to the altered expectations of engineers and managers today.

Is middle management an increasingly precarious career path, and might managers need to reskill and return to hands-on technical work – or even consider retirement? Will makes the case, and we hear why the traditional path to engineering executive roles is changing, as well as why taking one step backward might sometimes be the best way forward.

We discuss Will’s early career, and get his first-hand account of Digg’s disastrous relaunch, his own path to CTO, and he tells us why career ladders still matter. We also explore how AI is changing engineering roles and bringing technical decision-making back to leadership.

Takeaways from the conversation with Will

Here are some standout talking points from our conversation, during which Will recommends middle managers to go back to line management and re-skill like he has done. He didn’t ask me to, but I want to mention that he’s hiring for several key engineering manager roles at Imprint to use agents to rethink how software teams work.

1. Will shares an inside account of how a 10 website sank into irrelevance after a v4 rewrite. Digg was the “king” of social media sites in the late 2000s; bigger than Reddit, and one of top-10 most visited websites, globally. That all crashed to a halt in 2010 when the company embarked on a massive rewrite called Digg v4 – and it was a disaster. It was the start of Digg’s downfall.

Will worked at Digg during this rewrite, and shares how Digg was already losing traction and traffic to Facebook, and that Google changed its algorithm which caused 60-70% traffic loss. From the outside, Digg looked like it was growing, but its business prospects were shrinking fast. The company had about 120 people and was burning through money fast.

Into this entered the v4 rewrite, which was carried out to a hard deadline set by Kevin Rose, the newly-returned CEO at the time. The v4 version alienated passionate users, and had major performance and reliability problems.

Will and a small engineering team fixed the issues. The root cause was Python memory leaks introduced by devs who didn’t know Python so well. Will has shared more detail on his blog.

Even so, Will doesn’t think the rewrite killed Digg: with or without that rewrite, Digg would’ve met the same fate of being overtaken and replaced by Facebook and Reddit.

2. At Yahoo, a “black market” for servers popped up after the cofounder insisted on personally approving new servers. A hilarious story of how incentives drive behavior: Yahoo cofounder, David Filo, wanted to drive accountability by teams justifying every server purchase. This created a “black” market and Will recalled that one engineer on his team had 30 servers left from a canceled project that he traded with devs who could not get approvals elsewhere, in exchange for stuff he needed. Also, servers didn’t have to be returned, so Yahoo ended up running a large number of outdated, power-hungry machines!

3. In the 2000s, having annual 1:1s with managers was normal. Will worked at Yahoo in 2008-2010 and had two 1:1 sessions with his manager: one in which they asked Will about someone else’s performance, and the next one when he handed in his notice after it finished. It was pretty common for 1:1s with managers to be rare things at the time.

4. Too many Staff+ engineers only want to work on fun problems. At Stripe, Will led an org of about 250 people, where lots of the most senior engineers regularly sought more “engaging” problems to work on. Will eventually found his optimal response:

“I only have suffering to offer, but this suffering is what’s going to make the business succeed.”

However, he felt that he was seen by some as guilty of violating an unwritten rule of management by not finding enough – or interesting enough – problems for them to engage with. Today, at Staff+ levels, engineers putting business problems first is a baseline expectation.

5. ZIRP shaped engineering management practices in the 2010s, Will believes. ZIRP stands for zero interest rate period – and we did a deepdive on the impact ZIRP had on engineering management. He recommends the article ‘ZIRP explains the world’ by Ranjan Roy. From Will:

“Back then, your ability to hire and close and retain became the differentiator between successful companies. The less successful ones simply couldn’t retain great people.

[This dynamic on hiring and retaining] pulled leverage back into the engineer’s hands and created a very different environment. So, companies were pitching themselves as a more relaxed environment, more focused on you, and offering more career development. And I think in ways that I think were often kind of self-defeating.”

6. “Hire more engineers” used to be the answer from many engineering leaders in the 2010s. Today, it’s not, he says:

“I tell my teams that I work with now that hiring is the least interesting way to solve every problem. We should almost never talk about hiring.

But in the 2010s, we basically told managers they couldn’t think about technological solutions. And then what do they have? They have process solutions, they have scheduling, or they have people to hire.”

7. Focus on engineering wellbeing could have led to less reliable software. During the 2010s, several companies chose to not put the highest-paid engineers oncall, and for it to be handled by others. But when engineers are oncall for the software they build, it leads to better, more reliable software. Back then, not having oncall was a way to hire and retain talent, but it also led to lower quality as engineering teams did not feel the pain of outages caused by their own software.

Side note from Gergely: I wonder if AI agents will make a difference here. One of the worst things about oncall is getting awoken by the pager. Could we design loops that automatically mitigate incidents that we expect and are well-prepared for?

8. Software engineering change is more extreme, and it’s driving away some engineers. Will knows someone who decided to retire from tech because AI has destroyed the ability to be “in the flow.” Engineers are being more productive, but enjoy it less. By focusing on the outcomes, Will says he’s having a great time.

9. The tech lead manager role is now very in demand. Will wrote previously about how the tech lead manager role is a career trap, and I have a similar opinion in the deepdive ‘Engineering leadership skillset overlaps:’

Things are changing inside companies; EMs are starting to manage 12-14 people, instead of 4-8, as before, while Directors are managing more TLMs. At Imprint, some of Will’s best hires have been managers who also want to write software. The TLM role is perfect for this. In his book, he describes a great TLM as someone who has the capability, but no desire, for bureaucratic work; by default, they’re builders.

10. Engineering managers used to expect not to make technical decisions, but that’s outdated now. Will recalls:

“One of the worst parts of being an engineering manager in the 2010s was when you joined the ranks of engineering management, one of the first lessons you’d get was: ‘you need to never make a technical decision again.’ That’s literally what I was told.”

It was the same advice I received when becoming an EM: let your engineers make the technical decisions, get out of their way, and support them in growth. The tide is very much changing these days, with more tech companies expecting managers to be hands-on and in the details.

11. Great engineering executives (CTOs, VPEs) need to be technologists and bureaucrats. Will believes an engineering executive has two jobs:

  • Be a bureaucrat: manage incentives, create and deal with bureaucracy, and know how to navigate it. The job often includes running functions you know nothing about

  • Be a technologist: know what to build, how it works, and whether a technology choice makes sense or not

Will reckons that until recently, many engineering executives from the middle-manager path were bureaucrats before they were technologists.

12. Blunt message for middle managers: retire or re-skill. Will left a team of 250 at Carta to head up 25 tech people at Imprint. He purposely took a “step back” in his leadership career because he believes things are changing so radically that the engineering leadership profession that we know will not exist in three years.

Amid all this, Will says that line management can be a lot more engaging for executives these days because the tools for line management and the tools for writing software are really good. However, the tools of bureaucracy are still pretty terrible, he believes. That’s why some talented engineering folks get jaded about the work:

“For a lot of folks, there is this sense the industry has betrayed them and that they’re owed something that they’ve worked for. And the thing is, they’re right!

They have worked incredibly hard, but the rules have changed. Since the 2010s, we’ve forgotten that our industry is actually very volatile. We really do just get paid to do things that are valuable to the companies. There’s no entertainment orientation to why these companies employ us.”
